objective: Expect the parsed DOM to differ from the source markup, and inspect the tree when diagnosing structure.

original.explanation: The HTML parser inserts an implied `tbody` around rows written straight inside `table`, since the `tbody` start tag is one HTML lets you leave out, so the DOM holds an element the source does not. That is why a selector like `table > tr` does not match rows written that way, and why a structural bug is diagnosed in the inspector rather than by rereading the template: the markup is valid, and no build step or extension is involved.

rationale: Provide exact markup and a text/html parsing context instead of guessing whether a build tool or extension changed an unspecified page. Keep the parser explanation concise.

objective: Identify the containing block of position: absolute: the nearest positioned ancestor, else the initial containing block.

original.hint: The parent is not automatically the reference. Ask what an ancestor must have for an absolutely positioned child to measure from it.
original.question: What is `position: absolute` positioned relative to?
options: The nearest positioned ancestor, else the initial containing block
Its direct parent, in every case
original.explanation: An absolutely positioned box is placed relative to the padding box of its nearest ancestor whose `position` is anything other than `static`; if there is none, the initial containing block — the viewport-sized rectangle at the top of the document — is used. A dropdown that escapes to the page corner is nearly always this: the intended ancestor was never given `position: relative`. An ancestor with a `transform` or `filter` also becomes the containing block, which is a separate surprise.

rationale: The original correct option ignored transformed or otherwise containing-block-creating ancestors,even though its explanation mentioned them. Scope the positioning-only rule explicitly.

objective: Read the inset shorthand: inset: 0 sets all four offsets, stretching an auto-sized absolute box across its containing block.

original.hint: Name the four longhands `inset` stands for. Then ask what an absolutely positioned box with `auto` width does when both of its horizontal edges are set.
original.question: What does `inset: 0` on an absolutely positioned element do?
options: Adds zero padding on all four sides
Sets all four offsets to 0, stretching it across its containing block
Centres it inside its containing block
Sets a zero margin on all four sides
original.explanation: `inset` is the shorthand for `top`, `right`, `bottom` and `left`, so `inset: 0` pins all four edges to the containing block. With `width` and `height` left `auto`, an absolutely positioned box solves for its size from the pinned edges and fills the block — the standard overlay. It has no effect on non-positioned elements, and it is not padding, margin or centring (centring needs `margin: auto` on top of it).

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: Remove unconditional stretching from the answer:that depends on dimensions,replaced status and margins. Test the shorthand’s direct effect and state the common overlay assumptions separately.
evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Properties/inset
